opening.say: Say a car's odometer reads a hundred miles at noon, and a hundred and sixty at one o'clock.
Sixty miles in an hour is easy. But what was the speedometer showing at exactly noon, one single instant?
Let's write the car's position as a function of time, and see how we could pin down that instant.

more.say: Say the car's position follows a simple rule: distance equals t squared. After two hours it's four miles out.
Between two hours and three hours, it covers five miles. That's an average speed of five miles per hour.
But the car was slower at the start of that hour and faster at the end, so five isn't the speed at any one moment.

plan.setup: Watch the line as the second point slides closer.
plan.narration: [[curve-appears]]Here's position over time. [[secant-line]]Pick two points and draw a line through them. Its slope is average speed. [[points-merge]]Now slide the second point toward the first. [[tangent-line]]The line settles into a tangent. [[slope-label]]That tangent's slope is the derivative: the speed at one instant.
plan.plan:
curve-appears: a smooth upward curve of position against time is drawn, equal to t squared.
secant-line: two points on the curve, a straight line through both, rise and run marked; its slope is the average rate.
points-merge: the second point slides along the curve toward the first, and the secant line visibly rotates.
tangent-line: the line becomes the tangent touching the curve at exactly one point locally, matching the curve's direction.
slope-label: the tangent's slope is labeled as the derivative, the instantaneous rate of change, the limit of the average rates.
plan.close: If the tangent line is flat at some point, what's the derivative there?
